new_statements.quote: Modern Galo exhibits a strongly falling rhythmic preference, leading to a robustly trochaic (strong-weak) meter at the level of the phonological word. [...] Since Galo is a weight/quantity-sensitive language (i.e., it treats “heavy” and “light” syllables differently), the precise outcomes of these two processes are different [...]. Importantly, however, only the final syllables of a disyllabic phonological word are affected; initial syllables of disyllabic phonological words, whether heavy or light, receive a stress accent and do not undergo any restructuring processes. [...] such phenomena are indicative of a trochaic stress pattern, in which initial syllables are fortified due to stronger metrical prominence, and final syllables are reduced due to lower metrical prominence.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is initial: the (prototypically disyllabic) phonological word is a trochee, strong-weak; the first syllable carries the stress accent regardless of its weight, while the word-final syllable is metrically weak and undergoes syncope/apocope and vowel reduction. Galo additionally has two lexical word-level tones (H, L) whose surface domain is the same phonological word; syllable weight matters for the reduction outcomes, not for the position of the accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said; the article treats only mono- and disyllabic phonological words (longer grammatical words are parsed into several phonological words per Post 2009). Foot iteration in longer words is described only in Post 2007 sec. 4.1.4 (not opened).
new_statements.exceptions: None for accent placement. Weight-sensitivity governs how final syllables reduce (CVV length neutralised phrase-finally; short final vowels reduced phrase-medially; final CVC nuclei reduced); 'Triggered foot-strengthening' geminates the onset of the final syllable when a vowel-initial enclitic attaches to a bimoraic word (tabə + =ə > tabbə), fortifying the stressed initial syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (prototypically disyllabic, bimoraic minimum), not the grammatical word; reduction of the weak final syllable differs in phrase-final vs phrase-medial position, and citation forms count as phrase-final. Data are Lare Galo. The author is the writer of the reference grammar (Post 2007) and explicitly summarises its ch. 4 here, so the statement is first-hand though the paper is typological/historical in purpose.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand statements (Post 2006, 2007, 2011) describe the Lare dialect of Galo (lower Siyom/Aalo area); Post 2006 fn.6 says the trochaic foot is also observed in the Pugo dialect. Glottolog 5.1 lists no dialect-level codes under galo1242, so galo1242 is the right key. Galo is also a lexical tone language (two word-level tones, H and L, TBU = phonological word), so the stress statement co-exists with tone.

sources.note: Sec. 6.2 (p.211): modern (Lare) Galo has a strongly falling rhythmic preference, a robustly trochaic (strong-weak) meter at the level of the phonological word; sec. 6.2.2.1 (p.212): Galo is weight-sensitive, but initial syllables of disyllabic phonological words, heavy or light, receive a stress accent and never reduce, only final syllables syncopate/apocopate; sec. 6.3 (p.214): these phenomena indicate a trochaic stress pattern (initial syllables metrically prominent). Refers fuller description to Post 2007 sec. 4.1.4.6 (Triggered foot-strengthening) and Post 2009.
